newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand says won't borrow to solve finance woes.
newsitem.headline: Thailand says won't borrow to solve finance woes.

text.p: Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said on Wednesday that the government will not borrow from abroad to solve liquidity problems in the financial sector.
He also told reporters that the government will announce more measures to bail out the troubled financial sector on July 28 but declined to elaborate.
Thailand recently ordered the suspension of 16 troubled finance companies and forced them to consolidate with stronger ones as a step to shore up its ailing finance sector.
Thanong said Thailand would be able to solve current problems without resorting to government borrowing. He stressed that any borrowing should be done by the private sector.
Thai laws restrict public borrowing and requires that when government-to-government borrowing is made, the borrower must provide specific details on how the money will be spent.
"The government does not want to borrow to create unnecessary burdens, and it will be difficult to say which companies we have to help," he said.
"It's the private sector that has liquidity problems, therefore it should borrow and handle the situation while the government supports them with various measures," he said.
The minister recently ruled out market speculation that Thailand may seek an IMF financial package or take loans from Japan to overcome current economic problems, the worst in over a decade.
Thanong repeated that Thailand would not need a financial package from the IMF now as what it has done and plans to do to solve its financial crisis was in line with IMF recommendations.
IMF's first deputy managing director, Stanley Fischer, said on Monday that Thailand needs tax, banking and currency measures to cope with the aftermath of the baht currency crisis.
He said some measures had already been taken, but the country could face a long period of slow growth if action was not decisive.
